audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Dutch Law bachelor teaches the main fields of Dutch law through legal problems and small-group work. Students also study European and international law and complete an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The comparison uses the 2026–2027 curriculum. One UCR plan combines comparative law with politics and argumentation. The other studies how law relates to social issues. Maastricht provides a fuller sequence in Dutch law and legal practice.

cellNotes.text: Both introduce legal traditions and ways of thinking about law. UCR also examines law as a social institution.
Both draw on history and philosophy. UCR focuses on the foundations of human rights. Maastricht also covers legal theory and the psychology of law.
Both introduce private law. UCR uses comparative examples in property, tort and contract. Maastricht introduces the Dutch system of private rights and obligations.
Both study contracts and remedies. UCR focuses on cross-border commercial transactions and arbitration. Maastricht studies Dutch obligations more broadly, including tort and unjust enrichment.
Maastricht studies jurisdiction and choice of law in cross-border private disputes. UCR covers related commercial disputes within Transnational Business Law.
UCR studies property within Principles of Private Law. Maastricht provides a separate course.
Maastricht provides dedicated study of Dutch company and insolvency law.
Maastricht provides a dedicated course on property between partners and succession.
Maastricht provides a dedicated Dutch employment law course. UCR addresses employment in the context of transnational business.
Maastricht provides a dedicated course on Dutch civil procedure.
Both study limits on government power, rights and judicial review. UCR compares legal systems and covers administrative law within that comparison.
UCR covers public authority and administrative remedies within comparative constitutional law.
UCR covers this area within Comparative Constitutional Law, paired below with Maastricht’s combined constitutional and administrative law course.
Maastricht provides a separate course on administrative procedure. UCR covers administrative remedies and procedural fairness within Comparative Constitutional Law.
Public Economics covers taxation and redistribution. Maastricht studies tax law.
Both study criminal liability and the principles of criminal law. Maastricht also introduces criminal procedure.
Maastricht extends the study of criminal law and criminal procedure in Year 3. UCR covers core criminal law in a single course.
Both introduce the sources and subjects of international law. Maastricht also introduces EU law in this course.
UCR examines EU institutions, competences, legal sources and enforcement. Maastricht combines EU law with further study of public international law.
Both develop first-year academic and professional skills. Maastricht includes coaching and portfolio work across a three-year sequence.
Maastricht trains students to read legal sources and reason through Dutch legal problems. UCR develops related argument skills across several courses.
Maastricht continues training in legal argument and interpretation of Dutch legal sources.
Maastricht has a further module in practical legal skills.
Maastricht continues its coached professional skills sequence in Year 2.
Maastricht completes its professional skills sequence in Year 3.
Students can use the final 12 EC for an internship, faculty or external courses, or an approved project or research option.
Maastricht requires a research proposal and an individual thesis. UCR methods courses develop empirical research skills, and optional independent research sits outside the scheduled courses.

notes.text: Maastricht builds depth in Dutch private, public and criminal law and legal procedure over three years. UCR offers a comparative introduction to several legal fields and uses politics, philosophy and sociology to examine how legal institutions work.

Maastricht requires a legal skills sequence and an individual thesis. The 12 EC of final-semester electives can include a legal internship. UCR’s optional independent research is separate from the scheduled coursework.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENBUSI211.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
BENBUSI211.text: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. Students study AI's capabilities and limits, applications across business functions and industries, and effects on labour markets, productivity, innovation and inequality. Business cases and scholarly arguments support analysis of governance, regulation and a country's AI readiness and industrial policy.

Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

ENSDELT211.name: Living with Water
ENSDELT211.text: Studies water risks and opportunities in deltas, using Zeeland as a central case. Flooding, freshwater scarcity, salinisation, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, then apply these ideas through site-based inquiry and a project on delta adaptation.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.
